title: $3.7B cash and the $20B capex bar
body:
## The FY2025 Inflection

When Nebius published its fourth-quarter 2025 results on 12 February 2026, the numbers removed any remaining ambiguity about the company's ambitions. [Q4 revenue came in at $227.7 million, up 547 percent year-on-year](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results). The core AI cloud segment grew 802 percent. The company exited the year with an annualised revenue run rate of $1.25 billion and $3.7 billion of cash on the balance sheet. In the final quarter alone, Nebius deployed approximately $2 billion of capital expenditure. Active connected power reached 170 megawatts against more than 2 gigawatts of contracted future capacity.

The quarter's revenue figure came in below consensus expectations of roughly $247 million. That miss mattered less than the direction of travel. Guidance for FY2026 — revenue of $3 to $3.4 billion, capital expenditure of $16 to $20 billion, ARR of $7 to $9 billion with more than half already contracted — was the most aggressive full-year commitment any publicly listed AI cloud company had issued. The equity market's reaction was to price the guidance, not the miss.

## The Prepayment Signature

The most structurally important disclosure in the Q4 print was not on the income statement. [Operating cash flow for the quarter totalled $834 million against reported revenue of $227.7 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm) — a ratio of approximately 3.7 times.

That gap is the fingerprint of hyperscaler-style customer prepayment. Enterprise and research customers paying for future GPU compute capacity in advance generate cash immediately; that cash is recorded as deferred revenue and recognised only when capacity is consumed. The dynamic is structurally familiar from AWS and Azure reserved-instance arrangements and from CoreWeave's disclosed prepayment terms. At Nebius, the Q4 ratio — cash collected running at 3.7 times revenue recognised — indicated that a substantial book of forward commitments had been signed and partially funded heading into 2026.

The implication for the FY2026 guidance was direct. When management described more than 50 percent of the $7 to $9 billion ARR target as already contracted at guidance issuance, they were not projecting from pipeline probability. They were projecting from signed agreements with cash-deposit mechanics already in motion. The operating cash flow dynamics offered partial corroboration that characterisation was accurate at year-end 2025.

## Walking the Guidance Arithmetic

The FY2026 guidance represented one of the most concentrated tables of forward financial commitments in the AI-infrastructure sector.

| Metric | FY2025 Reference | FY2026 Guidance | Implied Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $227.7M (Q4 run-rate) | $3.0–$3.4B | ~7× FY25 |
| ARR (exit) | $1.25B | $7–$9B | 5.6–7.2× |
| Capex | ~$2B (Q4 alone) | $16–$20B | — |
| Connected power | 170 MW | 800 MW–1 GW | 4.7–5.9× |
| Adj. EBITDA margin | 24% (Q4 2025) | ~40% | +16 pp |
| Contracted ARR share | — | >50% | — |

[Source: Nebius Q4 2025 6-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm)

The revenue guidance of $3 to $3.4 billion implied approximately seven times FY2025 revenue at the midpoint. That growth rate was not plausibly modelled as speculative pipeline in February 2026; it required the contracted-ARR coverage already embedded in the signed book to convert into delivered capacity and recognised revenue on schedule across the year.

The ARR target of $7 to $9 billion is a forward-looking exit figure — the run rate the company intended to reach by 31 December 2026. Working backward: if exit ARR reaches the $8 billion midpoint, Q4 2026 revenue would approach $2 billion in a single quarter — seventeen times the Q4 2024 base. Management commentary in the [earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) indicated more than half of that range was contracted at issuance, providing a structural floor beneath the headline figures rather than a speculative ceiling.

## The Capex Arithmetic

The most challenging line in the guidance was capital expenditure: $16 to $20 billion for FY2026 against projected revenue of $3 to $3.4 billion. That is a capex-to-revenue ratio of between 4.7 and 6.7 times — a ratio with no parallel in the history of publicly listed AI cloud infrastructure at this revenue baseline.

Nebius was not building incrementally against existing utilisation. It was constructing capacity ahead of demand — acquiring and fitting out data centre facilities, executing GPU procurement with Nvidia, and activating power utility agreements, all simultaneously. In Q4 2025 alone, approximately $2 billion of capital expenditure was deployed against $227.7 million of revenue: a 9-times single-quarter ratio. The FY2026 guidance implied this pace would not only continue but accelerate. On a straight-line basis, $16 to $20 billion over four quarters averages $4 to $5 billion per quarter — a doubling to two-and-a-half times the Q4 2025 quarterly rate.

The build-ahead-of-demand model is structurally sound only if contracted ARR converts. Infrastructure purchased to fulfil commitments that slip or cancel becomes stranded depreciation. The fact that customer prepayments were already generating $834 million of operating cash flow in a single quarter against $227.7 million of recognised revenue was, in the Q4 print, the single most important signal that contract quality was sufficient to justify the commitment pace.

## The Financing Stack

At year-end 2025, Nebius held $3.7 billion in cash and liquid equivalents. That figure reflected the accumulation of the August 2025 $700 million strategic equity placement — conducted at an oversubscribed close — alongside the conversion of contracted ARR into advance-payment receipts through the year.

The participants in the August 2025 placement were publicly disclosed as Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts managed by Orbis Investments. Accel's Matt Weigand received observer rights at the transaction close and was subsequently elected to the board at the August 2025 annual general meeting. Nvidia's participation formalised what had previously been an implied supply relationship: as the dominant GPU vendor to the AI cloud sector, Nvidia's equity stake in Nebius aligned the interests of infrastructure customer and hardware supplier in a way that carried structural implications for allocation priority during periods of constrained supply.

Against a capex guidance of $16 to $20 billion, the $3.7 billion year-end cash position covered between 18 and 23 percent of the low-to-high range. Management guidance acknowledged explicitly that the capex programme exceeded cash on hand and that additional financing — through customer prepayments, potential debt issuance, or further equity — would be required during the year. The operating cash flow dynamics suggested customer prepayments were already partially absorbing this gap, but the magnitude of the buildout required at least one additional capital-markets transaction within the guidance window to fund full execution.

The strategic-investor structure of the August 2025 placement reframed the equity story at a critical moment. Coming within months of the company's operational re-listing on NASDAQ as Nebius Group, an oversubscribed close with named institutional and corporate participants — one of them the world's most valuable semiconductor company — provided a de facto validation certificate from the infrastructure investment community precisely when market credibility was most consequential.

## The Margin Mechanics

The adjusted EBITDA margin trajectory deserves separate treatment because it is the mechanism through which the operating model becomes self-reinforcing at scale.

Nebius reported adjusted EBITDA margin on its core AI cloud segment of 19 percent in Q3 2025. In Q4 2025, [that figure expanded to 24 percent](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm) — a 5 percentage point sequential expansion in one quarter as fixed operating costs began to distribute across a faster-growing revenue base. The FY2026 guidance targeted approximately 40 percent adjusted EBITDA margin — 16 percentage points above the Q4 2025 exit rate. Reaching 40 percent requires that revenue growth materially outpaces incremental operating expenditure in areas like headcount, customer support, and network operations, while the buildout spend is captured in capex and depreciation below the adjusted EBITDA line.

The Q4 net loss of $249.6 million illustrates why the GAAP income statement is a lagging and partial indicator of operating health at this stage of the ramp. A significant portion of that loss reflects depreciation on infrastructure deployed ahead of the revenue curve and non-cash stock-based compensation associated with the management team reconstituted after the 2024 restructuring. The $834 million operating cash flow figure, by contrast, reflected the business's actual cash-generation capacity in a quarter when customer commitments were converting to advance payments faster than infrastructure could be recognised as revenue — a divergence that understates economic progress on the GAAP income statement and overstates it on nothing at all; it simply reflects the timing architecture of the prepayment model.

## The Power Problem — and What It Signals

The connected power trajectory is, in some respects, the most legible proxy for execution progress available to external observers. Software and contractual commitments are difficult to audit from SEC filings; megawatts of activated data centre power are not.

Nebius reported 170 megawatts of active connected power at year-end 2025 against more than 2 gigawatts contracted across its facility portfolio. The FY2026 guidance called for 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt of active connected power by year-end 2026 — a 4.7-fold to 5.9-fold expansion in activated physical capacity in twelve months, a rate with few precedents outside hyperscaler construction programmes operating at dramatically larger absolute scale.

The 2-gigawatt contracted figure provided a ceiling: Nebius had secured the utility agreements and site commitments to support the guidance target in principle. The execution question was whether activation of that contracted capacity could be paced to match Nvidia GPU delivery schedules and customer deployment timelines. In an environment where GPU allocations remained a binding constraint for AI infrastructure capacity, the August 2025 equity investment by Nvidia was directly relevant: a supplier with a financial stake in the customer's growth carries a material incentive to prioritise that customer's allocation requests.

At 170 megawatts active against 2 gigawatts contracted, Nebius ended 2025 with roughly 8.5 percent of its contracted capacity producing revenue. The gap between that figure and the 40-percent-plus EBITDA margin target for 2026 describes the entire financial story the numbers were telling — a company that had secured commitments far in excess of its current operating footprint, had begun to activate that footprint at pace, and was committing $3.7 billion of cash plus the most aggressive public guidance in the sector to the proposition that the activation curve would prove as steep as the revenue and ARR projections required.
